title: Drowning: rescue and first care
asks: someone is drowning how do I rescue them
pulled from the water and not breathing
kid went under in the lake and is unresponsive
do I pump the water out of the lungs
how to save a drowning person without drowning myself
pt submerged pulled out not breathing
he swallowed water and is coughing is he ok
answer: Call for help, and keep yourself safe: rescuer safety is a priority. An untrained rescuer or weaker swimmer should use flotation devices, ropes or paddles instead of swimming to the person.

Rescue options: reach with an object from the shore or boat; throw a rope or something that floats; row or paddle a small craft to them; tow them to shore. Go into the water only as a last resort, and only if it is within your skill.
Out of the water, place the person so that the head and feet are at the same level.
If the person is unconscious and not breathing: begin with 5 rescue breaths, then continue with 30 chest compressions and 2 rescue breaths, repeated.
Sweep sand, seaweed or other material out of the mouth with a finger only if you can see it.

An unconscious person who cannot keep their own airway open should be placed in the recovery position (on their side) to reduce the risk of breathing in vomit. Vomiting is common with rescue breaths and CPR after drowning: use the recovery position whenever you are able.
Keep the person warm: dry and insulate them to prevent heat loss.

Everyone who needed resuscitation, even rescue breaths alone, should go to a hospital for evaluation and monitoring, even if alert and stable. Also evacuate anyone who was unresponsive in the water or has trouble breathing or other breathing symptoms.
warnings: Do not use abdominal thrusts (the Heimlich maneuver) or a head-down position to get water out: they decrease ventilation and increase the risk of vomiting. The Heimlich maneuver has no role unless a solid object (not water or vomit) blocks the airway and breaths cannot otherwise get in.
After drowning in cold water, rewarm the person while CPR continues: no victim should be declared dead until they are rewarmed and fail to respond to CPR.
In the water, chest compressions are not effective and should not be attempted. Give rescue breaths in the water only when the person cannot be got out quickly.
Do not delay rescue breaths to immobilize the neck unless the circumstances suggest a spinal injury (diving, boat accident, fall from height).
Start resuscitation unless there are clear signs of death: people have survived prolonged submersion, especially in cold conditions.
After immersion in water, breathing problems can develop several hours later: watch the person closely.

quotes.text: Rescuer safety is a priority. Untrained rescuers or weaker swimmers should utilize alternative means of rescue such as the use of flotation devices, ropes, or paddles.

1. Reach with an object from the safety of the shore or ship. 2. Throw an object like a rope or flotation devices (this may help the victim stay afloat or the search and rescue team locate the victim.) 3. Row (or paddle) a smaller craft to the victim if they are too far from shore to reach or have a floatation device thrown. The rescuer should ideally stay out of the water. 4. Tow them into shore or away from danger in the water (i.e. swift water rescue). 5. Go into the water (as a last resort) to rescue the victim if this is within the rescuer's skill set.
In water rescue, breaths should only be done when rapid extraction is NOT feasible. In water, chest compressions are NOT effective and should not be attempted.

Call for help and encourage patient to move away from danger.16-17 ▪ Place the patient so that the head and feet are at the same level. If rescuing a patient from the shoreline, place them parallel to the shoreline. ▪ Airway, Breathing, Circulation. If unconscious and not breathing, begin with 5 rescue breaths, then continue with traditional basic life support utilizing a ratio of 30 compressions and 2 rescue breaths. Five breaths are used initially as a recruitment maneuver. Drowning patients without circulatory arrest will often respond to rescue breaths alone.

Rescue breaths and CPR represent significant risk of emesis in drowning victims (65% of those requiring rescue and 88% of those receiving chest compressions).10 Placing patients in the recovery position as able can reduce the risk of subsequent aspiration.

All victims of drowning who require resuscitation (including rescue breathing alone) should be transported to the hospital for evaluation and monitoring, even those who are alert and demonstrate hemodynamic and respiratory stability at the scene of initial injury.

Aggressive resuscitation attempts should be initiated unless clear signs of death or as limited by operational requirements. Patients have survived prolonged submersion historically, especially in the hypothermic environment.

Assess patency of the patient's airway; consider foreign bodies unique to drowning injuries such as sand or seaweed and perform finger sweep if there is a visible obstruction. ▪ If the patient is unconscious and unable to maintain their own airway, place the patient in the recovery position (lateral recumbent) to minimize risk of aspiration.
Avoid head down positioning or abdominal thrusts as they decrease ventilation and increase risk of vomiting, which can lead to aspiration. Heimlich maneuver is NO LONGER recommended for drowning.

Keep the victim warm (use core temperature instead of infrared devices - a low range refrigerator thermometer may be necessary). Stabilize body temperature - dry and insulate the patient to prevent heat loss.

Evacuation: Evacuate if victim required resuscitation, was unresponsive in the water, or has dyspnea or other respiratory symptoms. ▪ Continue resuscitation and transport to higher level of care unless there are obvious signs of death.

Unnecessary cervical spine immobilization can impede delivery of rescue breaths via time of application and reduced airway opening. Routine stabilization of the cervical spine in the absence of circumstances that suggest a spinal injury (diving, boat accident, and fall from height) is not recommended.
Following immersion in water (drowning), a person may develop late signs of breathing problems after several hours and should be observed closely.

In clearing the airway prior to CPR, do not perform the Heimlich maneuver! The Heimlich maneuver has no role in drowning resuscitation, unless a solid foreign body obstructs the airway (this does not mean water or vomit) and ventilation is otherwise impossible.
Hypothermic near-drowning victims should be rewarmed while CPR is ongoing, and no victim should be declared dead until they are rewarmed and fail to respond to CPR or other resuscitative efforts.

conflict: WHEN TO STOP (the card gives no stop time): JTS Drowning Management 2025 says in-water rescue becomes body recovery after more than 60 minutes of submersion, resuscitation of a non-hypothermic patient may stop after 30 minutes of CPR without return of circulation, and a hypothermic patient is rewarmed to 30-34 °C before stopping if still without a heartbeat for more than 20 minutes; HHS Ship's Medicine Chest 2003 says no victim should be declared dead until rewarmed and unresponsive to CPR. NECK: JTS says routine neck immobilization is not recommended unless the circumstances suggest spinal injury (diving, boat accident, fall from height); Ship's Medicine Chest says remove the victim carefully, protecting the neck in the event of spinal injury (compatible). PULSE CHECK: Ship's Medicine Chest says check breathing and pulse for a full minute if the victim has been in cold water; JTS gives no time. FEMA P-2064 (2020) has no drowning first aid.

review.notes: Confirmed in context: JTS Drowning Management 2025 (rescuer safety; reach-throw-row-tow-go; no compressions in water, breaths only if extraction is slow; head and feet level; 5 rescue breaths then 30:2; vomiting and recovery position; finger sweep only if visible; no head-down or abdominal thrusts; keep warm; hospital for anyone resuscitated; evacuation criteria; no routine neck immobilization; resuscitate unless obvious death), WHO (late breathing problems), HHS (no Heimlich unless solid object; rewarm during CPR, not dead until warm). Call for help is first. Stop-time, neck and pulse-check differences are listed. No PDF junk. Recommended: JTS also says 'Drowning patients without circulatory arrest will often respond to rescue breaths alone'; add 'if there is a pulse, keep giving rescue breaths only' so compressions are not started on a beating heart (same gap as cpr-adult); HHS's full-minute pulse check in cold water is worth showing on the card.
